Tuesday. Farhan called from the bus stop, breathless: the theatre company in Pune wanted him for its six-week residency. Ganga squealed so loudly her roommate looked up. Then, after the call, she sat quietly. Six weeks. Their anniversary fell right in the middle.
Following Saturday. She helped him pack, rolling his kurtas the way he never could. At the station he kept apologising. "Stop," she said, grinning. "You're going to be brilliant. Go."
Three weeks later. Anniversary night, on a video call. Farhan was still in costume, glowing, telling her about the standing ovation. Ganga had eaten dinner alone. She listened, chin on her hands, and realised she was smiling harder than he was.

qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when she sat quietly after the first call?
qa.a: Ganga was thrilled for Farhan but also a little sad, since six weeks apart meant missing their anniversary together.

qa.q: At the station Farhan kept apologising. Why was Ganga's reply a good choice?
qa.a: By telling Farhan to stop and go be brilliant, Ganga freed him to enjoy the chance without guilt, which shows a secure, generous love.

qa.q: What might it mean to Farhan to see Ganga smiling on the anniversary call?
qa.a: Farhan would likely feel deeply supported, able to share the joy fully without feeling he had let Ganga down. ❤️

passage: Irawati, you ask why I keep that yellowed newspaper cutting. Sit. I was twenty-one, married only a year, when your Thatha's name appeared in it: first in the state in the engineering service exam. It meant a posting in Assam for two years, and I would stay here with his parents. Everyone expected me to cry. Your Sarika Ammamma did cry, for one night. But in the morning I cut out that article and pinned it by the stove, and every time I made tea I read his name again and felt like a lamp had been lit inside me. His joy was my joy. I missed him terribly. I was also so proud I could barely sit still. Both, kanna. Love can hold both.

qa.q: Where was Thatha posted after the exam?
qa.a: In Assam, for two years.

qa.q: What did Sarika Ammamma feel each time she read the cutting by the stove?
qa.a: Sarika Ammamma felt lit up with pride and joy for Thatha, even while missing him terribly.

qa.q: What choice did Sarika Ammamma make the morning after crying, and what did it do?
qa.a: Pinning the cutting by the stove turned a day of loss into a daily reminder of Thatha's success that she could share in.

qa.q: How might Irawati see the old cutting after hearing this?
qa.a: Irawati may now see it as a sign of deep, secure love rather than just an old newspaper, and understand why Ammamma kept it.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being joyful and proud at twenty-one when her husband's success took him away for two years.

passage: The monsoon had flooded half the ring road, and Zubin's scooter died two kilometres from the college auditorium. He pushed it the rest of the way, soaked to the knees. Inside, Afreen was on stage holding a giant cardboard cheque: first prize in the student startup pitch. The prize meant three months of mentorship, weekends included. Their Goa trip, planned since January, was now off. Zubin didn't care. Dripping at the back of the hall, he whistled so loudly people turned round. Afreen saw him, laughed, and pointed. Later, over cutting chai, she said, "Sorry about Goa." Zubin shook his head, rain still in his hair. "Goa will be there. You were amazing up there. I've never been this happy for anyone."

qa.a: Two kilometres from the college auditorium.

qa.q: How can you tell Zubin was truly happy for Afreen?

qa.q: When Afreen apologised about Goa, what did Zubin's reply do?
qa.a: It told Afreen the win mattered more than the trip, so she could enjoy the success without guilt about the weekends it would take.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel seeing Zubin dripping at the back of the hall?
qa.a: Afreen would probably feel touched and supported, seeing Zubin make such an effort just to cheer.

grounding: A young man beams at a friend's startup win even though it cancels their long-planned trip.

passage: Aparna burst into their Hyderabad flat waving her phone. "The research lab in Bengaluru! They took me for the summer!" Rukmini dropped the dosa batter spoon and screamed. They hopped around the kitchen together. It was the lab Aparna had emailed three times. That night, lying awake, Rukmini remembered their summer plan: the train to Hampi, the cheap guesthouse she'd already bookmarked, two months of lazy mornings. All gone. She waited for resentment to show up. It didn't, really. There was a small pang, but mostly she kept replaying Aparna's face in the kitchen, lit up like a lamp. In the morning Rukmini opened her laptop and started a list for Aparna: hostels near the lab, a list of good cheap dosa places in Bengaluru, and a note: Hampi in December?

qa.q: What was Rukmini and Aparna's summer plan?
qa.a: The train to Hampi, a cheap guesthouse and two months of lazy mornings.

qa.q: What does Rukmini keep replaying as she lies awake, and what does it suggest?
qa.a: Aparna's face lit up like a lamp; it suggests her joy for Aparna is stronger than the pang of losing their summer.

qa.q: Which choice in the morning shows secure affection, and why?
qa.a: Making a list of hostels and dosa places for Aparna, and suggesting Hampi in December, supports her friend's plan while keeping their own.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel seeing Rukmini's list?
qa.a: Aparna would likely feel deeply supported and relieved that her news didn't hurt their friendship.

"Eshaan! You're late again. Your dal's cold."
"Sorry, sorry. Coach kept us for extra drills." Eshaan dropped his kit bag in the hostel room doorway, grinning. "He says I might start in the first match."
"Start? As in, first eleven?" Chinmay jumped up off the bed.
"First eleven."
"Dude!" Chinmay grabbed him by both shoulders and shook him. "That's the national university tournament!"
"It means practice every evening till November. No more cooking nights. No more gaming."
"So? You've wanted this since first year."
"You're not annoyed?"
Chinmay thought for a second. "I'll miss burning rotis with you. But look at your face right now. I'd trade a hundred cooking nights for that face."
Eshaan laughed, embarrassed.
"Now eat your cold dal, star player."

qa.q: Until when will Eshaan have practice every evening?
qa.a: Till November.

qa.q: What does Chinmay's line about trading cooking nights reveal about his feelings?
qa.a: It shows Chinmay truly delights in Eshaan's happiness, despite missing their evenings together.

qa.q: What would you advise Chinmay to keep doing through the season?
qa.a: Keep cheering, maybe come to matches, and find small times to connect, so the friendship stays warm while Eshaan is busy.

qa.q: Why might Eshaan have asked "You're not annoyed?"
qa.a: He likely worried his success would cost the friendship, and was relieved and a bit embarrassed by Chinmay's warmth.

grounding: A young adult is delighted by a friend's selection even though it takes their evenings away.
